```{python}
#| echo: false
import json
from pathlib import Path
from scripts.config import PROJECT_ROOT

RESULTS = json.loads((PROJECT_ROOT / "outputs" / "results.json").read_text())
F = RESULTS["focal"]
AID = RESULTS["aid_curve"]

def usd(x, dec=0):
    if x is None:
        return "n/a"
    return f"-${abs(x):,.{dec}f}" if x < 0 else f"${x:,.{dec}f}"

def pct(x, dec=1):
    return f"{x*100:.{dec}f}%"

def ratio(x, dec=1):
    return f"{x:.{dec}f}x"
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**The bottom line.** A Stanford education is simultaneously one of the most
expensive in America — a sticker price of `{python} usd(F['sticker_cost'])` — and, for
the students who actually need help, one of the most affordable. The average
student pays a net price of `{python} usd(F['net_price_avg'])`, and families earning
under $30,000 pay a **negative** net price. What Stanford sells — and what it
costs — depends almost entirely on who is buying.
:::

# One university, two price tags

The College Scorecard publishes two numbers for every school: the **sticker
price** (published tuition, fees, room and board) and the **net price** (what
students actually pay after grants and scholarships). For Stanford, the gap
between them is enormous.

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Sticker price

In 2024-25 the full cost of attendance at Stanford was
`{python} usd(F['sticker_cost'])`. That is `{python} ratio(F['multiples']['cost_vs_national'])` the median
sticker price across all four-year colleges — a price point shared only with
the nation's most selective private universities.

![Full cost of attendance, Stanford vs. peer elite privates.](./figures/fig_sticker_cost.png){#fig-sticker}

#### What families actually pay

But almost nobody pays the sticker. Grants and scholarships pull the average
net price down to `{python} usd(F['net_price_avg'])` — *below* the national median net
price of `{python} usd(F['national']['median_net_price'])`. The sticker is a ceiling;
the net price is the real number, and it falls steeply as family income falls.

![Average net price by family income bracket, Stanford and peer median.](./figures/fig_aid_curve.png){#fig-aid}
:::

# Aid that follows need — and a middle-class squeeze

Stanford's aid policy is aggressively need-based. For the poorest families the
math produces a surprising result: a **negative** net price, because aid
packages are large enough to exceed the full cost of attendance.

| Family income (dependent students) | Stanford net price | Peer median |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| $0–30,000 | `{python} usd(AID['stanford']['$0–30,000'])` | `{python} usd(AID['peer_median']['$0–30,000'])` |
| $30,001–48,000 | `{python} usd(AID['stanford']['$30,001–48,000'])` | `{python} usd(AID['peer_median']['$30,001–48,000'])` |
| $48,001–75,000 | `{python} usd(AID['stanford']['$48,001–75,000'])` | `{python} usd(AID['peer_median']['$48,001–75,000'])` |
| $75,001–110,000 | `{python} usd(AID['stanford']['$75,001–110,000'])` | `{python} usd(AID['peer_median']['$75,001–110,000'])` |
| $110,001+ | `{python} usd(AID['stanford']['$110,001+'])` | `{python} usd(AID['peer_median']['$110,001+'])` |

The result is a curve that looks like a ski jump: from a *negative* price for
the poorest families to `{python} usd(AID['stanford']['$110,001+'])` for the richest.
That `{python} usd(AID['stanford']['$110,001+'] - AID['stanford']['$0–30,000'])` swing
across the income distribution is the second-sharpest in the peer group,
essentially tied with Caltech and trailing only the University of
Pennsylvania's.

The sticker price, in other words, mostly tells you what *wealthy* families
pay. The families who need help get a very different — and far better — deal.

# The tuition engine

None of this is new. Published tuition at Stanford has been compounding faster
than inflation for a quarter century.

```{python}
#| echo: false
T = {row["series"]: row for row in RESULTS["trend"]["tuition_series"]}
SF = T["stanford"]; PEER = T["peer_median"]
```

From `{python} SF['start_year']`-01 to `{python} SF['end_year']`-25, tuition rose from
`{python} usd(SF['start_nominal'])` to `{python} usd(SF['end_nominal'])` — up
`{python} pct(SF['nominal_growth_pct']/100, 0)` in nominal terms and
`{python} pct(SF['real_growth_pct']/100, 0)` after inflation. That is fast. It is also,
tellingly, almost exactly what Stanford's peers charge: its 15 peer institutions
saw real tuition growth of `{python} pct(PEER['real_growth_pct']/100, 0)` over the same
period.

![Published tuition, 2000-01 to 2024-25, in real 2025 dollars.](./figures/fig_cost_trend.png){#fig-trend}

What stands out is not the *rate* of growth but the **level**. Stanford and its
peers did not just inflate tuition together — they inflated a shared price
point that the rest of American higher education never approached. National
median published tuition, pulled down by community colleges and regional
publics, is a rounding error next to it.

# What the price buys

High price tags are easier to justify when they buy completion. Stanford
graduates **`{python} pct(F['grad_rate_150'])`** of its entering class within six years
— a number most colleges would kill for, yet the *lowest* among its 15 peer
institutions, where six-year rates routinely clear 94%.

Debt is where Stanford's economics get friendlier. Among borrowers, median
cumulative debt is `{python} usd(RESULTS['debt']['stanford']['grad_debt_median'])` —
about half the national median of
`{python} usd(RESULTS['debt']['national_median']['grad_debt_median'])`. Low-income
graduates who borrow leave with a median of `{python} usd(F['lowinc_debt_median'])`.

![Median graduate debt, low-income vs. high-income borrowers.](./figures/fig_debt_by_income.png){#fig-debt}

The borrow-less story is a function of both generous aid and the fact that the
typical Stanford family doesn't need loans. The same pattern holds across the
peer group — a reminder that "debt-free graduation" at elite institutions is
less a policy achievement than a measure of who gets in.

# The payoff: a 47% earnings premium

The number families actually want is what graduates earn. Ten years after
enrollment, the median Stanford graduate earns **`{python} usd(F['earn_median_p10'])`** —
about `{python} ratio(F['multiples']['earnings_vs_national'])` the national median
of `{python} usd(F['national']['median_earnings_p10'])`.

![Distribution of earnings for Stanford and all four-year colleges.](./figures/fig_earnings.png){#fig-earnings}

The right tail is what separates Stanford from merely well-compensated schools.
The 90th percentile of Stanford graduates earns `{python} usd(F['earn_p90_p10'])` — a
figure that outranks all but Harvard, MIT, and Penn in the peer set. An elite
brand, in other words, buys not just a higher floor but an exceptionally high
ceiling.

# How much of that is the school — and how much the students?

```{python}
#| echo: false
R = RESULTS["regression"]
FR = R["focal_residual"]
COEFS = {t["name"]: t for t in R["terms"]}
```

A naive reading of the earnings chart is that Stanford *produces* six-figure
careers. A fairer question is whether Stanford is selecting for them. We can
test that with a regression over the `{python} f"{R['n']:,}"` four-year
colleges in the ROI sample that have complete records for every predictor in
the model (net price, selectivity, and family income) — a narrower group than
the 1,079-school ROI sample used elsewhere, since this model needs all five
variables at once, not just net price and earnings: how much do graduates
earn, *given* a school's net price, selectivity, and the average family
income of its students?

The model explains about `{python} pct(R['r_squared'], 0)` of the variation in median
earnings across schools. Three predictors dominate:

- **Student family income** (`DEP_INC_AVG`) is by far the strongest — a
  one-standard-deviation increase in the average family income of a school's
  students is associated with roughly
  `{python} pct(COEFS['DEP_INC_AVG']['coef'], 0)` higher earnings.
- **Selectivity** (admission rate and average SAT) is significant but weaker.
- **Net price** adds essentially nothing once the others are included.

And yet Stanford still clears the bar. The model, fit on the *same* data,
predicts median earnings of `{python} usd(FR['fitted_dollars'])` for a school with
Stanford's profile. Actual median earnings are `{python} usd(FR['actual_dollars'])` — a
residual of about **`{python} pct(FR['residual_pct']/100, 0)` above prediction**.

![Earnings vs. net price across 1,079 four-year colleges, with Stanford and peers highlighted.](./figures/fig_roi_scatter.png){#fig-roi}

That residual is the honest center of the prestige debate. Stanford's graduates
out-earn what their inputs predict — but the largest input is the wealth of the
families who enroll. A substantial share of the "Stanford premium" is inherited
before a single class is attended. The 47% is what's left after accounting for
that, and it should be read with the usual caveat: these are averages over
observed cohorts, not causal effects, and they say nothing about what any
individual student will earn.

# The whole story in one chart

Stanford occupies a narrow corner of American higher education: near the top
of the cost distribution and near the top of the returns distribution, with a
financial-aid system that passes the wealth test better than almost anyone —
for the students it admits.

The broader lesson of the Scorecard is less flattering. Across all 2,379
four-year colleges in the analysis universe, sticker price, net price, and
graduate earnings are all driven by the same underlying variable: the wealth of
the students at the door. Stanford is the best-case version of that story — and
the version that makes the rest of the system's failures most visible.

## Data, methods, and caveats

- **Source:** U.S. Department of Education College Scorecard, June 2026
  release (most-recent-cohort institution file; historical archive 1996-97 to
  2025-26). CPI-U inflation adjustment via FRED (CPIAUCSL); all dollars
  expressed in 2025 dollars.
- **Universe:** 2,379 four-year, degree-granting public and private non-profit
  institutions (not all of them report cost data; see [Methods](docs/methods.qmd)).
  **Peer frame:** Stanford plus 15 elite private peer universities (16 schools
  total). **Earnings regression:** `{python} f"{R['n']:,}"` schools with
  matched net price, selectivity, family income, and earnings records — a
  narrower group than the 1,079-school ROI sample used for the scatterplot
  above, which only requires net price and earnings.
- Net prices are averages for dependent students in each income bracket.
  Earnings are for the cohort ten years after first enrollment (includes
  graduates and non-graduates).
- The residual analysis is descriptive and in-sample; it is not a causal
  estimate of the effect of attending Stanford.
- Full methods: [`docs/methods.qmd`](docs/methods.qmd). Reproduce everything
  with `make pipeline` (see [`README.md`](README.md)).
